rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse endorses Makkah’s pilgrimage rites and sacred places as Islamic practices already known in pre-Islamic Arabia.
rows.anchor: give Islamic endorsement to various sacred elements and rituals associated with Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shaʿāʾir can mean either the rites themselves or the places where they are performed.
rows.anchor: Shaʿāʾir can mean either “rituals” or “ritual places.”

rows.speaker: Ṭ and Z
rows.claim: They understand the command as recognizing all sacred rites and places connected with pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: The verse is understood as an injunction to recognize all the sacred rites and places associated with the pilgrimage (Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ reads the command as avoiding everything forbidden while in pilgrim sanctity.
rows.anchor: to avoid all things prohibited in a state of pilgrim sanctity (iḥrām; Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q and Ṭ
rows.claim: Q and Ṭ read it as requiring fulfillment of every element of the pilgrimage ritual.
rows.anchor: to fulfill all the elements of the pilgrimage ritual (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ also reports a broader reading in which violating God’s rites means disobeying all Divine commands and prohibitions.
rows.anchor: following all Divine commands and prohibitions in general (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran uses shaʿāʾir specifically for rites and sacred places of the Makkan pilgrimage, though later usage broadened it.
rows.anchor: the Quran employs shaʿāʾir exclusively in connection with the Makkan pilgrimage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Makkah’s precinct and Sacred Mosque were sanctuaries where violence and bloodshed were avoided, though fighting was allowed if Makkans initiated it there.
rows.anchor: was observed by refraining from violence or bloodshed in this area

rows.speaker: Q and R
rows.claim: They take the singular sacred month to denote all four traditional months of abstention from violence: Rajab, Dhu’l-Qaʿdah, Dhu’l-Ḥijjah, and Muḥarram.
rows.anchor: Some say that the reference to the sacred month in the singular here denotes all four sacred months

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran upholds the sacred months in the Islamic setting; fighting in them was permitted under certain conditions during the Muslim-Makkan conflicts.
rows.anchor: The Quran here and elsewhere (see 2:217; 9:36) upholds the sanctity of these months in the Islamic context as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also allowed fighting during the sacred months under certain conditions in the years of conflict.
rows.anchor: the Quran allowed for fighting during these months under certain conditions

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some consider the months’ sanctity abrogated, at least regarding fighting idolaters, by the command in 9:5.
rows.anchor: Some consider the sanctity of these months to be abrogated (at least in relation to fighting idolaters) by 9:5

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Late Quranic passages and the Prophet’s Farewell Pilgrimage address uphold the sacred months’ sanctity.
rows.anchor: in an address given by the Prophet during his Farewell Pilgrimage (IK), the sanctity of these months is upheld.

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Z says the sacred month here may specifically mean Dhu’l-Ḥijjah, when the major pilgrimage occurs.
rows.anchor: the sacred month in the present verse to refer specifically to Dhu’l-Ḥijjah, the month in which the major pilgrimage is performed (Z)

rows.speaker: R and Ṭ
rows.claim: R and Ṭ suggest that the month may specifically mean Rajab.
rows.anchor: it may mean Rajab (R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ also suggests that the month may specifically mean Dhu’l-Qaʿdah.
rows.anchor: Dhu’l-Qaʿdah, specifically (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command forbids harming or destroying sacrificial animals and violating their protected status, signified by garlands around their necks.
rows.anchor: the verse then forbids specifically harming or destroying the offerings

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q reports that garlands were used in pre-Islamic pilgrimage and regarded as an original Abrahamic practice.
rows.anchor: their use was considered to have been originally an Abrahamic practice (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those travelling to the Kaʿbah as pilgrims must be allowed to travel safely and peacefully.
rows.anchor: one must allow those bound for the Sacred House (i.e., pilgrims to the Kaʿbah) to travel in safety and peace.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some date the verse to after Makkah’s conquest but before 9:1–28 barred idolaters from pilgrimage, when they could still perform major or minor pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: this verse was revealed after the conquest of Makkah, but before the revelation of 9:1–28, which banned the idolaters from the Kaʿbah pilgrimage.

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ, and W
rows.claim: They report that the verse protected a Yamāmah man who had feigned interest in Islam, stolen Muslim camels, and later approached pilgrimage with the garlanded sacrificial animals.
rows.anchor: this verse was revealed in relation to a man who had once come to Madinah from Yamāmah feigning interest in embracing Islam

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ, and W
rows.claim: When Muslims recognized the man and stolen camels at pilgrimage, the revelation instructed them not to interfere with him or the offerings.
rows.anchor: they were not to interfere with the man or the sacrificial camels (Q, Ṭ, W).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After 9:1–28, idolaters no longer had these protections; this abrogated the ruling, not the text, insofar as it had applied to them.
rows.anchor: this represents a clear example of naskh (abrogation), where one Quranic verse abrogates the legal ruling (but not the text) of another verse.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ considers the verse’s universal protections abrogated only to the extent that they no longer applied to idolaters.
rows.anchor: protections of the sacred months and pilgrim status implied in this verse were therefore considered abrogated

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ says pilgrims may seek worldly gain through trade as well as spiritual benefit and God’s reward.
rows.anchor: people may make the ḥajj hoping both for worldly gain through trade or commerce conducted in the process and for the spiritual purpose of pleasing God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people who had turned believers away were former Makkan idolaters who expelled Muslims and blocked their ʿumrah attempt in 628.
rows.anchor: Those people who once turned the believers away from the Sacred Mosque are the former Makkan idolaters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse warns believers not to let old hatred lead them to violate converts’ rights or act unjustly toward them.
rows.anchor: the believers are warned not to allow any lingering ill will or hatred for them to lead them to transgress the rights of the new converts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet illustrated the converts’ full standing by giving them all spoils from a later victory, easing any resentment they might retain.
rows.anchor: the Prophet made the extraordinary gesture of giving all of the considerable spoils of this battle exclusively to the new Makkan Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The good things, especially food, are Divine provisions believers may enjoy and should receive with gratitude.
rows.anchor: Here and in v. 5, the Quran mentions the lawfulness of the many good

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Enjoying good things is linked throughout the Quran to Divine favor and a community’s spiritual purity.
rows.anchor: The freedom to enjoy all good things, however, is tied to notions of Divine favor and the spiritual purity of a religious community throughout the Quran.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After manna and quails, Israelites were told to eat the provided good things; 3:93 says all food was lawful before the Torah except what Israel self-forbade.
rows.anchor: After the manna and quails were sent to Moses and the Israelites in the desert, they were instructed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because of Israelite wrongdoing, some previously lawful foods were later prohibited.
rows.anchor: As a response to the “wrongdoing” of the Israelites, however, this changed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus brought spiritual renewal, confirmed the Torah, and made some formerly forbidden things lawful for Israelites.
rows.anchor: Jesus, who is said by the Quran to have brought a message of spiritual renewal for the Israelites and to have confirmed the Torah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad likewise made good things lawful for “them,” apparently the Jews in context, while the teaching also applies to Muslims.
rows.anchor: which, in context, seems to refer to the Jews, although it also applies to Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran criticizes both consuming unlawful things and arbitrarily declaring lawful provisions unlawful; such restrictions attributed to Arabian idolaters signal spiritual decadence.
rows.anchor: it also criticizes those who deem “unlawful”what God has made lawful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse permits hunting licit game with trained dogs, other animals, and birds such as falcons.
rows.anchor: This verse allows the use of dogs or other animals and birds, such as falcons, in hunting licit game.

rows.speaker: Ṭ and W
rows.claim: Although some traditions deem dogs unclean, this verse permits trained hunting dogs and by extension dogs used for protection or other valuable services; their impurity does not apply in such cases.
rows.anchor: it is thus understood that in such cases their unclean status does not apply (Ṭ, W).

rows.speaker: JJ and Ṭ
rows.claim: They explain teaching hunting animals as training them to obey human commands and catch prey without eating it.
rows.anchor: Teaching them from that which God has taught you refers to teaching them to obey human command and to catch prey without eating from it (JJ, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Caught prey is lawful if God’s name is spoken before releasing the hunting animal or over prey that remains alive.
rows.anchor: so long as one has pronounced the Name of God before releasing the hunting animal or over the prey that has been caught, if it is still alive.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Prey caught by an untrained wild or unknown animal, or partly eaten by the hunting animal, is unlawful because it shows inadequate training.
rows.anchor: because it indicates that the animal has not been properly trained (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, an animal eating part of the prey can indicate that it caught the prey for itself, making it unlawful to eat.
rows.anchor: because it indicates that the animal is considered to have caught it for itself.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ allows prey partly eaten by the hunting animal if the hunter reaches it alive, pronounces God’s name, and properly slaughters it under the exception in 5:3.
rows.anchor: then it is licit according to the exception established in v. 3 (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathūbatan normally means positive recompense, so introducing punishment with it is ironic and resembles the Quran’s announcement of punishment as glad tidings.
rows.anchor: Its use here to introduce Divine punishment is therefore ironic

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ explains God’s curse as exiling its recipients from Divine Mercy.
rows.anchor: Whomsoever God has cursed means those He has exiled from His Mercy (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apes likely allude to Sabbath-breaking Jews; apes and swine can metaphorically portray deliberate violators of religious Law in this world or the next.
rows.anchor: Among whom He made some to be apes is likely a reference to God’s having said to those Jews who violated the Sabbath

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Aj reads apes and swine as a changed, hardened heart prone to heedlessness.
rows.anchor: making them prone to heedlessness (

rows.speaker: Q and R
rows.claim: Q and R say the apes were Sabbath-breakers and the swine were Jesus’ followers who betrayed him at the Last Supper.
rows.anchor: Some say that apes refers to those who broke the Sabbath, and swine refers to those among Jesus’ followers who betrayed him during his last supper (Q, R).

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Z connects worship of false deities with Israelite worship of the golden calf.
rows.anchor: may refer to the Israelites’ worship of the golden calf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on killing game applies throughout both the major and minor pilgrimages.
rows.anchor: the ban on killing game while in a state of pilgrim sanctity is clearly stated and is understood as applying to those making either the major or the minor pilgrimage

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The prohibition is the actual killing; other pilgrims who eat the killed game owe no repentance or expiation.
rows.anchor: if other pilgrims were to eat from the killed game, no repentance or expiation would be incumbent upon them (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A dangerous animal may be killed when it immediately threatens human life, including lions, wolves, or scorpions.
rows.anchor: One is permitted, however, to kill an animal, not for food, but because it is immediately threatening to human life

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q reports revelation after a Madinan Helper’s 628 minor pilgrimage, when he killed a wild donkey.
rows.anchor: This verse was reportedly revealed after one of the Madinan Helpers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expiation is for intentional violations, excluding accidental killing and killing caused by forgetting one is in pilgrim sanctity.
rows.anchor: expiation is required from one who violates this ban intentionally—that is, not accidentally—or because he has simply forgotten that he is in a state of pilgrim sanctity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feeding the indigent and fasting are listed expiations also used for broken oaths; the pilgrimage setting makes an equivalent sacrificial offering the primary option.
rows.anchor: Several means of expiation are listed, including feeding the indigent and fasting, which, as already mentioned, are also means of expiation for broken oaths

rows.speaker: Q and Ṭ
rows.claim: Some say the offering’s equivalent may be monetary; it is brought to the Makkan sanctuary and distributed among its needy people.
rows.anchor: some say the monetary equivalent (Q, Ṭ), of the animal slaughtered as an offering brought to the Kaʿbah

rows.speaker: JJ and Q
rows.claim: JJ and Q explain that the offering is brought to the Makkan sanctuary for distribution to the needy there.
rows.anchor: that is, brought to the Makkan sanctuary

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The two just men assess the slaughtered animal’s value; that valuation sets the amount spent feeding the poor or the fast, one day per standard half-liter measure of its meat.
rows.anchor: their estimation of the worth of the slaughtered animal is also the basis of the extent of the other modes of expiation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hunting anywhere within Makkah’s sanctuary, even by nonpilgrims, and cutting its trees are prohibited; reports extend these rules to Madinah.
rows.anchor: Because of the sacred character of Makkah, hunting of any kind is not permitted within its precincts, even for nonpilgrims, and its trees may also not be cut.

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Reports and hadith also apply the Makkah sanctuary’s hunting and tree protections to Madinah.
rows.anchor: Some reports and aḥādīth apply these prohibitions to the city of Madinah as well.

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q says these sanctuary prohibitions have no expiation because this verse addresses only those in pilgrim sanctity.
rows.anchor: since the issue of expiation in the present verse relates only to those in pilgrim sanctity

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ interprets God’s forgiveness of past violations as forgiveness of illicit game killing during the pre-Islamic period.
rows.anchor: God has forgiven that which is past, that is, illicit killing of game done in the pre-Islamic period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title Mighty, Possessor of Vengeance is also used in three other verses.
rows.anchor: The description of God as Mighty, Possessor of Vengeance is also found in 3:4; 14:47; 39:37.

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q says the Prophet is to remind disbelievers of God’s sovereignty and power to destroy them by asking who owns the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is here instructed to remind the disbelievers of God’s Sovereignty and His ability to destroy them at will

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question may be rhetorical for Makkans: some acknowledged Allah as Creator despite mocking the Prophet, though not in the Abrahamic sense.
rows.anchor: The question may have been rhetorical for the idolatrous Makkans, since despite their mocking of the Prophet and the warning he brought, some did acknowledge Allāh as the Creator

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verse reiterates that everything belongs to God.
rows.anchor: That all things belong to God is then reiterated in v. 13.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s self-prescription of Mercy means that, while absolutely free, He has obligated Himself to act mercifully toward creatures.
rows.anchor: although God remains absolutely free, He has nonetheless obligated Himself to act with mercy toward His creatures.

rows.speaker: God
rows.claim: A sacred hadith says God decreed the created realm and wrote that His Mercy prevails over His Wrath.
rows.anchor: When God decreed the created realm, He prescribed for Himself in a Book that is with Him

rows.speaker: God
rows.claim: Another sacred hadith states that God’s Mercy has precedence over His Wrath.
rows.anchor: My Mercy has precedence over My Wrath.

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly prayed for refuge in God’s contentment from anger, forgiveness from punishment, and mercy from wrath.
rows.anchor: The Prophet reportedly would pray during his daily devotions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mercy is the dominant aspect of God’s relationship with creatures, as established by His self-obligation.
rows.anchor: Mercy is therefore the dominant aspect of God’s relationship with His creatures, as established by His own self-obligation.

rows.speaker: Q and Ṭ
rows.claim: They say God’s self-prescribed Mercy explains why He gives disbelievers respite to repent and believe instead of destroying them immediately.
rows.anchor: this statement that God has prescribed Mercy for Himself explains why He does not bring the punishment down upon the disbelievers immediately

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Z suggests God’s self-obligated Mercy may more generally mean He undertook to guide creatures to recognize His Oneness.
rows.anchor: His having undertaken to guide His creatures to an understanding of His Oneness (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among God’s Quranic Attributes, Mercy alone is said to be prescribed for Himself, giving it unique and supreme status.
rows.anchor: “Mercy” is the only one that He is said to have

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That God prescribes Mercy indicates it is intrinsic to Him, since only essential mercifulness could make Mercy a principle of His acts.
rows.anchor: Mercy is an intrinsic or essential quality of God, not merely a way of relating to His creatures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s Mercy continues in the Hereafter, while earthly respite and guidance eventually end when He gathers everyone for Resurrection.
rows.anchor: Although God’s Mercy continues into the Hereafter, the period of respite and guidance for human beings on earth will eventually come to an end

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Resurrection Day is repeatedly described as a day without doubt.
rows.anchor: Here and elsewhere, this day is described as one in which there is no doubt

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Z says those who lost their souls through associating equals with God, rejecting His signs, and mocking the Prophet’s message do not believe because of these ruinous beliefs and acts.
rows.anchor: their lack of faith can be seen as a result of these ruinous actions and beliefs (Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The statement recurs in 6:20; Ṭ says the lost-souls phrase may describe those whom God gathers on Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: some commentators read those who have lost their souls as a description of those whom God will gather . . . on the Day of Resurrection (Ṭ).
